extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor lawyers, unions, worker advocates, and regulators assessing FLSA worker classification
extracted.subtask_short: FLSA employee vs independent contractor test
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the FLSA's economic reality test to determine whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor, including critiques of the 2021 IC Rule and articulation of which facts and factors should be considered and how they should be weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of control indicative of an employment relationship (the 'control' factor) is one of the economic reality factors to be considered; it should not be elevated above other factors nor rigidly narrowed to only certain types of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat control as a 'core' factor automatically decisive of status. Consider the employer's right to control (not merely the actual control exercised by the worker). Do not exclude from consideration employer-imposed requirements such as legal obligations, health and safety standards, insurance requirements, contractually agreed deadlines or quality-control standards. Avoid analyzing control so narrowly that it focuses only on control exercised by the worker rather than the employer's reserved authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for profit or loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the worker has an opportunity for profit or loss from the work, based on the worker's initiative and/or investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat opportunity for profit or loss as a distinct factor. Consider whether the worker's initiative (business risk-taking, ability to increase profits) and the worker's investment affect profit/loss prospects. Avoid the 2021 IC Rule's approach that automatically equates presence of initiative or investment with independent contractor status without broader context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the investments made in the work/business by the worker and by the potential employer as part of determining economic dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disregard employer investments. Investment and opportunity for profit/loss should be examined as separate factors (consistent with Silk and most circuits). Consider both parties' capital, tools, facilities, and other investments when assessing whether the worker is in business for themself or dependent on the employer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral-part (centrality) factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the worker's services are an integral part of the potential employer's business — i.e., the importance or centrality of the work to the employer's operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt an unduly narrow inquiry (for example, limiting the question to whether the work is part of an 'integrated unit of production'). Courts have examined whether the work is an 'integral part' of the business; this broader inquiry should be preserved in the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer's reserved right to control
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of an employer's reserved right or authority to control the worker is relevant to classification and should not be downplayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The employer's reserved contractual or practical authority to direct or limit how the work is performed can indicate employee status even if that authority is not fully exercised. Avoid minimizing reserved rights as irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the-circumstances economic reality test
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a totality-of-the-circumstances balancing test that considers multiple economic reality factors together rather than giving predetermined weight to any single factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No 'core' factors or fixed-weight tiers: do not adopt the 2021 IC Rule's approach of automatically giving certain factors greater weight or creating a three-tiered weighting (core / non-core / additional). Courts historically use a multifactor, context-specific balancing test; the Department's guidance should align with that approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single factor determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: No single factor should be dispositive in determining whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor under the FLSA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess all relevant factors collectively; avoid rules or presumptions that make one factor (e.g., control or opportunity for profit) decisive in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not preclude consideration of relevant facts
rubrics_metrics.description: All facts that may be relevant to economic dependence should be admissible in the factor analysis; the test should not exclude categories of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rule language that narrows the analysis by excluding facts (examples of impermissible exclusions in the 2021 IC Rule include barring consideration of compliance-motivated controls, employer investments, and centrality of work). The analysis should permit a full consideration of facts that could bear on economic dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid collapsing distinct factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain separateness of historically distinct factors (e.g., investment vs. opportunity for profit or loss) rather than merging them such that information is lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not collapse 'investment' and 'opportunity for profit or loss' into a single inquiry (as the 2021 IC Rule did by treating investment only as part of opportunity). Preserve distinct inquiries to reduce loss of probative information and to reflect circuit practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with FLSA text and judicial precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's test and guidance should be consistent with the FLSA's statutory language (e.g., 'suffer or permit') and longstanding Supreme Court and circuit court economic reality jurisprudence, which has a broader scope than common-law control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adopting an analysis that effectively converts the FLSA test into the common law control test courts have rejected. Ground factor definitions and weighting in case law. When in doubt, follow the approach used by appellate courts and the Supreme Court rather than novel, untested frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of control implemented for compliance and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Control exercised or required by the employer for purposes of complying with legal obligations, safety standards, contractual or customer service standards may be indicative of control and should be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not automatically exclude employer-imposed requirements that stem from regulatory, contractual, or safety needs from the control analysis. The final rule signals that such control can be probative of employment status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and avoidance of ambiguous new concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory guidance should promote clarity and predictability rather than introduce ambiguous categories (e.g., 'core' vs 'additional' factors) or undefined weighting rules that create confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguous constructs that leave regulated parties and courts uncertain how to apply the test (examples of confusing constructs include undefined thresholds for how 'substantial' a likelihood must be when core factors align, or unclear relative probative value of 'additional' factors). Strive for guidance consistent with established judicial approaches to minimize litigation and uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of misclassification harms and distributive impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking should account for the real-world harms of worker misclassification — including lost wages, denial of FLSA protections, reduced access to benefits, and disproportionate impacts on women, people of color, immigrants, and other vulnerable groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the potential for harm to workers (wage loss, lack of overtime, loss of family-leave protections, diminished collective action ability, loss of benefits and safety-net access) as part of the policy justification for preserving a broad, inclusive test that reduces misclassification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider judicial reception and litigation risk
rubrics_metrics.description: When crafting regulatory standards, consider whether federal courts are likely to adopt or apply the rule and the risk of protracted litigation creating uncertainty for nationwide businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid promulgating novel standards that depart sharply from appellate precedent in ways likely to be ignored or rejected by courts, as that could produce conflicting standards, increased litigation, and regulatory uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incentives that encourage misclassification
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory tests should not create perverse incentives for employers to misclassify workers (for competitive advantage or cost savings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that rules which narrow the scope of relevant facts or elevate certain factors favoring independent-contractor classification could encourage a 'race to the bottom' and increased misclassification, harming workers and law-abiding employers.
